x: A flood is water overflowing onto land that is normally dry, from heavy rain, rivers bursting their banks, or other causes. The other options describe surge, dam failure or GLOFs alone.
t: Recall the definition of a flood.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Rashtriya Barh Ayog put the flood-prone area at about 40 million hectares. About 49 million hectares is a more recent estimate.
t: Discriminate the RBA figure from the recent one.

x: Both are true: GIS can show community vulnerability because it stores, models and analyses spatial data. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the capability explains the use.

x: Both are true: the Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission) was set up in 1976 and reported in 1980, and the CWC runs India's flood forecasting network.
t: Distinguish the year a commission was set up from the year it reported.
s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The National Flood Commission, commonly called the Rashtriya Barh Ayog, was set up in 1976 and submitted its report in 1980.
Statement B: The Central Water Commission maintains a flood forecasting network across India.

x: I, II and IV are correct: river floods follow heavy monsoon rain, urban floods come from poor drainage and lost wetlands, and coastal floods from surges and tides. III is false because GLOFs come from glacial lakes bursting.
t: Match each flood type to its cause.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Riverine or fluvial floods result from the overflow of rivers due to heavy monsoon rainfall.
II. Urban floods may result from poor drainage, heavy rain and encroachment on wetlands.
III. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods result from storm surge and high tides.
IV. Coastal floods may be caused by storm surge, cyclones and high tides.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: The CWC runs flood forecasting, NDMA sets policy, the Brahmaputra Board controls floods and erosion in the North-East, and NDRF/SDRF rescue and give relief. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match each body to its role.

x: The order is Mumbai (2005), Kedarnath (2013), Chennai (2015) and Kerala (2018). The answer is B, D, C, A.
t: Arrange the floods in time order.

x: Both are true: flood water spills out of rivers and water bodies and cannot be held, and floods are rapid-onset disasters.
t: Recall the nature of floods.

x: Odisha made the flood hazard atlas, based on satellite images of past floods from 2000 to 2018, to manage floods better. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each item to its detail.

x: All four are correct: floods are India's most frequent disaster and cause huge yearly losses of money, lives and crops.
t: Recall the flood impacts.

x: All four basins see river floods: the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Kosi and Godavari.
t: Recall the flood-prone basins.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The Ganga basin is commonly affected by riverine or fluvial floods.
II. The Brahmaputra basin is commonly affected by riverine or fluvial floods.
III. The Kosi basin is commonly affected by riverine or fluvial floods.
IV. The Godavari basin is commonly affected by riverine or fluvial floods.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: flash floods come from sudden heavy rain or cloudbursts, and they are common in the Himalaya and in cities. Where they happen does not explain their cause, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a place explains a cause.

x: Mumbai had the 944 mm deluge of July 2005, Chennai the December 2015 floods, Bengaluru the September 2022 ORR flooding, Hyderabad the October 2020 Musi floods and Delhi the July 2023 Yamuna floods, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv, e-v.
t: Link each city with its signature urban flood event.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Mumbai
(b) Chennai
(c) Bengaluru
(d) Hyderabad
(e) Delhi

List-II
(i) July 2005 deluge of 944 mm in 24 hours
(ii) December 2015 floods worsened by loss of wetlands
(iii) September 2022 flooding of the Outer Ring Road IT corridor
(iv) October 2020 floods as the Musi and city lakes overflowed
(v) July 2023 floods as the Yamuna reached a record level

x: The west coast faces coastal floods, Uttarakhand the 2013 Kedarnath cloudburst and Chorabari outburst, Sikkim the 2023 South Lhonak GLOF on the Teesta, and Assam the Brahmaputra's yearly floods, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Link each region with its defining flood event or type.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) West coast
(b) Uttarakhand
(c) Sikkim
(d) Assam

List-II
(i) Coastal floods from storm surge and high tides
(ii) 2013 Kedarnath disaster from a cloudburst and the Chorabari lake outburst
(iii) October 2023 South Lhonak lake GLOF on the Teesta
(iv) Recurrent riverine floods of the Brahmaputra

x: Both are true: the Rashtriya Barh Ayog recommended integrated flood management, and State water departments build flood-control works.
t: Recall who does flood control.

x: Both are true: Bihar's big 2008 flood happened because the Kosi embankment breached. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the cause explains the event.

x: NDMA's flood guidelines came in 2008 and its urban flooding guidelines in 2010, the Odisha atlas covers 2000–2018, and the Rashtriya Barh Ayog, set up in 1976, reported in 1980. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Arrange the flood milestones in time order.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Guidelines on Management of Floods
(b) Guidelines on Urban Flooding
(c) Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas: period covered
(d) Report of the Rashtriya Barh Ayog

List-II
(i) 2008
(ii) 2010
(iii) 2000–2018
(iv) 1980

x: The IMD defines a cloudburst as at least 100 mm of rain in one hour over about 20–30 sq km.
t: Recall the 100 mm per hour rule.

x: Option A is incorrect: cloudbursts usually happen at 1,000–2,500 m in mountains, not 500–1,000 m.
t: Recall the cloudburst altitude range.

x: Both are true: cloudbursts are very hard to forecast because they are so local. R explains A.
t: Ask whether locality explains the difficulty.

x: Orographic lifting pushes moist air up slopes, instability builds tall cumulonimbus clouds, monsoon air supplies moisture, and the water falls all at once when updrafts weaken. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Match each factor to its role.

x: I and II are correct: the Himalaya and the windward Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra) are cloudburst-prone. III is false because flood management includes preparedness as well as forecasting.
t: Watch for an excluded element.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The Himalayan region is vulnerable to cloudbursts because of steep slopes, orographic effects and monsoon conditions.
II. Parts of Kerala, Karnataka and Maharashtra are vulnerable because of intense monsoon rainfall on the windward side of the Western Ghats.
III. Flood management requires flood forecasting and warning, but disaster preparedness is not relevant.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: A cloudburst is a rapid-onset disaster, striking within minutes to hours.
t: Discriminate rapid-onset from slow-onset.

x: Heavy rain can cause flooding, prolonged rain landslides, landslides can block rivers and cause havoc downstream, and poor drainage worsens urban floods. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each factor to its effect.

x: Both are true: urbanisation and poor planning both make urban flooding worse.
t: Recall the causes of urban flooding.

x: Both are true: a cloudburst can cause both flash floods and landslides. They are separate effects, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether two effects explain each other.

x: Both are true: cloudbursts can rarely happen in the plains, caused by local convection.
t: Recall cloudbursts in the plains.

x: Two are the main secondary hazards of cloudbursts: flash floods and landslides. Thunderstorms accompany the cloudburst itself, and tsunamis come from undersea earthquakes, not rainfall.
t: Discriminate cause from effect.
s:
How many of the following are identified as major secondary hazards of cloudbursts?

1. Flash floods
2. Landslides
3. Tsunamis
4. Thunderstorms

x: Doppler radar detects intense rain cells in real time, nowcasting gives forecasts for the next few hours, orographic lifting forces moist air up slopes, and the cumulonimbus cloud releases the burst. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Separate forecasting tools from the physical causes of a cloudburst.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Doppler Weather Radar
(b) Nowcasting
(c) Orographic lifting
(d) Cumulonimbus cloud

List-II
(i) Detects intense rain cells in real time
(ii) Very short-range forecast for the next few hours
(iii) Moist air forced up steep mountain slopes
(iv) Towering convective cloud that releases the burst

Choose the correct code:

x: Option C is incorrect: the Leh cloudburst was in 2010. 2013 is the Kedarnath disaster.
t: Match each cloudburst to its year.

x: Option C is incorrect: hailstorms in India occur mainly before the monsoon (March–May) and in winter, not October–December, and are rare in the monsoon.
t: Recall the hailstorm season.

x: Both are true: hailstorms are local, short and intense, and hail is ice formed in strong thunderstorms. The definition does not explain all three features, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a definition explains all the features.

x: Maharashtra's hail areas are Vidarbha and Marathwada, central India's MP and Chhattisgarh, the north-west's Punjab to Himachal, and others include Bihar, Karnataka and Uttarakhand. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match each region to its States.

x: All four are correct: a hailstorm is not biological, an earthquake strikes suddenly (rapid-onset), drought is slow-onset, and climate change is making extreme convective events more frequent.
t: Discriminate rapid-onset from slow-onset hazards.

x: Both are true: strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds freeze raindrops, and repeated layers of ice make hailstones grow.
t: Recall how hail forms.

x: All three are correct: convective instability, moisture and updrafts are atmospheric factors, western disturbances are synoptic factors, and plateaus and hills boost convection.
t: Recall the causes of hailstorms.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Strong convective instability, abundant moisture and strong updrafts are atmospheric factors associated with hailstorms.
II. Western Disturbances and wind discontinuity lines are synoptic factors associated with hailstorms.
III. Plateaus and hilly regions enhance convection associated with hailstorms.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
